usage: 사실은 at the very front softens an honest reveal, like English 'actually'
사실 + 이에요 asserts something is objectively true
사실대로 = 'as it really is'; the suffix -대로 means 'in accordance with'
I want to know the truth.
사실 as the object of a verb takes 을
examples: 사실 저는 매운 음식을 못 먹어요.
Actually, I cannot eat spicy food.
Bare 사실 (no 은) at sentence start = a casual 'to be honest' before a confession
이 이야기는 사실이 아니에요.
This story is not true.
사실이 아니다 is the set phrase for 'is not true / is false'
사실은 오늘 그 얘기를 하려고 왔어요.
The truth is, I came today to talk about that.
사실은 + a -려고 왔어요 clause reveals a hidden real reason behind an action
nuance: 사실 (事實, 事 'matter' + 實 'real/true') literally means 'the real state of a matter', so it covers both the noun 'fact' and the adverb 'actually/in fact'. Compare it with 진실: 사실 is a neutral, verifiable fact ('it rained yesterday'), while 진실 is the deeper moral 'truth' you uncover behind lies, so a courtroom seeks 진실, but a weather report states a 사실. Also distinguish 진짜, which is the casual spoken 'really/for real' and an intensifier ('진짜 맛있어!'), whereas 사실 introduces information. The phrase 사실은 / 사실 at the head of a sentence is enormously common in conversation as a gentle 'to tell the truth' before a correction or confession. The English-speaker pitfall: do not use 사실 to mean 'really' as an intensity word — '진짜 추워요' (it's really cold) is natural, but '사실 추워요' shifts the meaning to 'actually, it's cold (contrary to what you thought)'. Keep 사실 for facts and reveals, not for emphasis.

usage: 비밀 + 이에요 labels information as private
비밀을 지키다 = 'protect/guard a secret', the standard collocation
비밀이 없다 with the subject particle states you hide nothing
비밀로 하다 = 'treat it as secret'; -로 marks the resulting state
examples: 친구한테 비밀을 말했어요.
I told my friend a secret.
한테 marks the human recipient you told it to
그것은 우리만의 비밀이에요.
That is a secret just between us.
우리만의 = 'ours only'; -만의 stacks 'only' + possessive
이건 너랑 나만 아는 비밀이야.
This is a secret only you and I know.
Casual 반말 register with friends; 너랑 나만 = 'only you and me'
nuance: 비밀 (祕密, 祕 'hidden/mysterious' + 密 'dense/close') paints a secret as something kept tightly closed in. The verb it lives with is 지키다 ('to guard/keep'), giving 비밀을 지키다 — note that English 'keep a secret' tempts learners to reach for 가지다 ('to have/hold'), but 비밀을 가지다 sounds wrong; you 지키다 (guard) a secret, or 비밀로 하다 (make it secret). Contrast 비밀 with 비결: both share 비(祕), but 비결 (祕訣) is a 'secret know-how / the trick to success' (성공의 비결 = the secret to success), not confidential information. So a chef's 비결 is their technique, while their 비밀 might be that they hate cooking. The word is register-neutral and used freely from children's games to government affairs. Pitfall to avoid: 비밀 is a noun only — there is no verb 비밀하다. To say 'keep something secret' you must add a verb: 비밀로 하다 or 비밀을 지키다.

usage: 규칙은 sets 'rules' as the topic being discussed
규칙을 지키다 = 'observe/abide by rules', the core collocation
규칙이 많다 describes a place full of rules
examples: 학교 규칙을 잘 지켜요.
I follow the school rules well.
규칙 takes a noun modifier directly: 학교 규칙 = school rules
회사마다 규칙이 달라요.
Each company has different rules.
-마다 = 'each/every'; pairs naturally with 다르다
규칙을 어기면 벌금을 내야 해요.
If you break the rule, you have to pay a fine.
규칙을 어기다 = 'break a rule', the antonym of 지키다
nuance: 규칙 (規則, 規 'compass/standard' + 則 'rule') evokes a measured standard you align to, and its life-partner verbs are 지키다 ('keep/observe') and its opposite 어기다 ('break/violate'). The sharp contrast learners need is 규칙 vs 법: 규칙 is a rule set by a group, school, or game (게임 규칙, 교통 규칙), enforceable socially, while 법 (法) is the law of the land, enforced by the state with courts and penalties. Breaking a 규칙 gets you scolded; breaking a 법 gets you arrested. Also distinguish 규칙 from 규정 (規定), which are formal written 'regulations/provisions' in an official document — a workplace handbook lists 규정, but a casual house rule is a 규칙. Collocations: 규칙을 정하다 (set rules), 규칙대로 하다 (do it by the rules). Pitfall: English 'follow the rules' often becomes 규칙을 따라가다 by literal translation, but the idiomatic verb is 지키다 — 규칙을 지키다. Save 따르다/따라가다 for following a person or path.

usage: 좋은/나쁜 + 습관 describes the quality of a habit
I want to fix a bad habit.
습관을 고치다 = 'correct/break a habit'; 고치다 = repair
습관이 되다 = 'turn into a habit', now automatic
I have a habit of going to bed early.
verb + -는 + 습관이 있다 = 'have the habit of ~ing'
examples: 아침마다 운동하는 습관이 있어요.
I have a habit of exercising every morning.
-는 습관이 있다 is the frame for stating any routine
커피를 마시는 습관을 바꿨어요.
I changed my coffee-drinking habit.
습관을 바꾸다 = 'change a habit' (swap it), milder than 고치다
손톱을 물어뜯는 버릇이 안 고쳐져요.
I can't break my nail-biting habit.
Here a small bad tic is a 버릇, not 습관 — note the register difference
nuance: 습관 (習慣, 習 'to practice/learn' + 慣 'to grow accustomed') frames a habit as something drilled in until it feels natural, and it leans slightly formal and neutral. The key contrast is 습관 vs 버릇: 습관 is a broad, often deliberate routine (early rising, daily exercise, good study habits), while 버릇 is colloquial and usually a quirky or annoying unconscious tic — nail-biting, leg-shaking, a child's bad manners. Crucially, scolding a child you say 버릇없다 ('has no manners / is rude'), never 습관없다. Both pair with 고치다 ('fix') for breaking them and 들이다/생기다 for forming them (습관을 들이다 = cultivate a habit; 습관이 생기다 = a habit forms). To say you have one, use 습관이 있다. Pitfall: English 'I have a habit of doing X' must use the verb's -는 present-modifier form before 습관: 일찍 자는 습관 (the habit of sleeping early), not 일찍 자기 습관. Also do not use 가지다 here — habits 있다/되다/생기다, they are not 'had' with 가지다.

usage: 성격은 + adjective describes a fixed trait
성격이 좋다 = 'is good-natured/easygoing', a common compliment
성격이 비슷하다 compares two people's natures
밝다 ('bright') applied to 성격 = cheerful and warm
examples: 제 친구는 성격이 아주 활발해요.
My friend has a very lively personality.
활발하다 ('active, lively') is a stock 성격 adjective
성격이 달라서 가끔 싸워요.
Because our personalities differ, we sometimes argue.
-아서/어서 links the trait to its consequence
저는 성격이 급해요.
I'm impatient by nature.
성격이 급하다 = a fixed temperament; contrast with the mood word 기분
nuance: 성격 (性格, 性 'nature/disposition' + 格 'character/frame') is a person's enduring inborn character — the stable temperament you are born with and keep for life. Contrast it carefully with 기분, which is a passing mood that changes hourly: '오늘 기분이 좋아요' = I'm in a good mood today (temporary), whereas '성격이 좋아요' = he's a good-natured person (permanent). Mixing these is the single most common error: never use 성격 for how you feel right now. The phrase 성격이 좋다 is a warm social compliment meaning kind, tolerant, easy to get along with — broader than English 'good personality'. Note also 성격이 급하다 ('impatient/hot-tempered nature') is an idiomatic fixed expression. Common partner adjectives: 밝다 (cheerful), 활발하다 (lively), 조용하다 (quiet), 까다롭다 (fussy/picky), 무뚝뚝하다 (blunt). Pitfall beyond the 기분 trap: 'I have a ~ personality' is most naturally 성격이 + adjective (성격이 밝아요), not the heavier 저는 ~한 성격을 가지고 있어요 calque, though 급한 성격이에요 is fine.

usage: 능력이 있다 = 'has ability', i.e. is competent
I want to build up my ability.
능력이 부족하다 = a humble admission of falling short
noun + 능력 names a specific competence: 언어 능력 = language ability
examples: 그 사람은 일하는 능력이 뛰어나요.
That person's work ability is outstanding.
-는 능력 = 'the ability to ~'; 뛰어나다 = excel
저는 한국어 능력을 키우고 있어요.
I'm building up my Korean ability.
Ongoing -고 있다 with the develop verb 키우다
능력보다 노력이 더 중요해요.
Effort matters more than ability.
능력보다 = 'compared to ability'; -보다 marks the standard
nuance: 능력 (能力, 能 'can/be able' + 力 'power/force') is literally 'the power to be able' — innate or acquired capability to actually get things done, broader and more practical than book knowledge. Its verbs are 있다/없다 (have/lack), 키우다 ('raise/develop'), and 기르다 (cultivate). Contrast 능력 with 실력: 실력 is demonstrated skill/proficiency in a specific domain that you trained for (그 선수는 실력이 좋다 = that player is genuinely skilled), while 능력 is overall capacity, including raw potential and the power to handle responsibility. A new hire may have 능력 (capability/potential) but not yet 실력 (proven skill). Also distinguish 가능성 ('possibility'), which is the abstract noun 가능 + 성 — a chance that something happens, not a person's power. Pitfall: English 'I'm able to ~ / I can ~' should not be forced through 능력. To say 'I can swim', use the verb pattern 수영할 수 있어요, not 수영 능력이 있어요 (which sounds like a formal assessment). Reserve 능력 for describing overall competence, not everyday 'can do'.

usage: 실수하다 = 'to slip up'; the noun + 하다 acts as one verb
실수 + 예요 to own up to an error
I make a lot of mistakes.
실수가 많다 describes a tendency, not one event
실수를 하다 split out, with the negative command -지 마세요
examples: 오늘 회사에서 실수를 했어요.
I made a mistake at work today.
Everyday accidental slip; 실수를 하다 with location 에서
작은 실수니까 괜찮아요.
It's a small mistake, so it's fine.
-니까 gives the reason for reassurance
깜빡하고 이름을 잘못 썼어요. 제 실수예요.
I spaced out and wrote the name wrong. My mistake.
Real apology context — 실수 fits an honest, blameless slip
nuance: 실수 (失手, 失 'to lose' + 手 'hand') literally means 'to lose control of one's hand' — a slip, a careless unintended error, with no moral blame attached. This is the crucial contrast with 잘못 (잘 'well' + 못 'cannot'), which means a 'wrong/fault' that carries responsibility or wrongdoing: 실수 is 'oops, I tripped on the word', while 잘못 implies 'I did something wrong and it's my fault'. When you bump someone you say 실수예요 ('sorry, my slip'); when you genuinely wronged them you admit 제 잘못이에요. Also distinguish 실패 ('failure'), which is not achieving a goal, versus 실수, a momentary error along the way — you can make a 실수 and still succeed. The verb is 하다 (실수하다), and a frequent collocation is 실수로 ('by accident/mistake': 실수로 전화했어요 = I called by mistake). Pitfall: English speakers say 실수를 만들다 ('make a mistake') by translating 'make' literally — Korean does not 만들다 (build) a mistake, it 하다 (does) one: 실수를 하다 / 실수하다.

English speakers say 실수를 만들다 ('make a mistake') by translating 'make' literally — Korean does not 만들다 (build) a mistake, it 하다 (does) one: 실수를 하다 / 실수하다.

Using 실수 when you mean genuine fault or wrongdoing. A blameless slip is 실수; an actual wrong you're responsible for is 잘못 — 제 잘못이에요 for a real apology.
Confusing 실수 with 실패. Forgetting one line is a 실수 (a slip); not passing the whole exam is 실패 (a failure). They are not interchangeable.

usage: 성공하다 = 'to succeed'; noun + 하다 forms the verb
성공이 + adjective treats success as the topic
성공하다 + -고 싶다 to state an aspiration
성공하다 takes 에 for the field you succeed IN, not 을
examples: 오랜 노력 끝에 성공했어요.
After long effort, I finally succeeded.
-끝에 = 'at the end of ~'; pairs with effort then success
성공하려면 계속 노력해야 해요.
To succeed, you must keep trying.
-려면 = 'if you want to ~'; sets up advice
시험에 합격해서 정말 기뻐요.
I'm so happy I passed the exam.
For passing a test Koreans say 합격, not 성공 — note the boundary
nuance: 성공 (成功, 成 'to accomplish' + 功 'achievement/merit') means achieving a goal or making it big in life, and its verb is 하다 (성공하다), the natural antonym of 실패하다 ('to fail'). A grammar point English speakers stumble on: 성공하다 governs the particle 에 (or 에서) for the domain — 사업에 성공하다 ('succeed in business'), 시험에 성공하다 is odd; you say 시험에 합격하다 instead. This is the sharp contrast: 합격 (合格) is specifically 'passing' an exam, audition, or qualification screening, while 성공 is broad life or project success. Passing the bar exam is 합격; building a thriving company is 성공. Both differ from 성취 (成就), the more literary 'accomplishment/attainment' of a personal achievement. Common collocations: 크게 성공하다 (make it big), 성공을 거두다 (achieve success, formal/written). Pitfall: do not pair 성공하다 with the object particle 을/를 for the thing you succeed at — it's 에 (시험에 합격, 사업에 성공). And use 합격, not 성공, the moment you mean passing a test.

mistakes: Saying 시험을 성공했어요 for 'I passed the exam'. Use 합격: 시험에 합격했어요. 성공 is for broad goals/business, not test results.
Marking the domain with 을/를: 사업을 성공했어요 is wrong. 성공하다 takes 에: 사업에 성공했어요.

usage: 실패하다 = 'to fail (at a goal)'; noun + 하다
실패는 as topic, softening the concept
실패를 두려워하다 = 'fear failure'; 두려워하다 takes 를
실패하다 takes 에 for the area you failed in
examples: 처음에는 실패했지만 다시 도전했어요.
At first I failed, but I challenged it again.
-지만 = 'but'; 도전하다 (take on) fits the resilience tone
실패에서 많이 배웠어요.
I learned a lot from failure.
실패에서 = 'from failure'; 에서 marks the source
실패해도 괜찮으니까 한번 해 보세요.
It's okay to fail, so give it a try.
-아도 괜찮다 ('even if ~, it's fine') is gentle encouragement
nuance: 실패 (失敗, 失 'to lose' + 敗 'defeat') literally 'to lose and be defeated' — the failure to reach a goal, the clean antonym of 성공 (성공 ↔ 실패). Like 성공하다, the verb 실패하다 governs the particle 에 for the domain: 사업에 실패하다 ('fail in business'), 시험에 실패했어요 is possible but Koreans far more often say 시험에 떨어졌어요 ('I fell off the exam' = flunked) for not passing. That is the contrast to master: 실패 is broad, often big-picture failure, while 떨어지다 is the everyday idiom for failing a test or audition (the opposite of 합격). The big distinction for learners is 실패 vs 실수: 실수 (失手) is a small careless slip you make in passing, whereas 실패 is the larger non-achievement of an outcome — you can commit many 실수 and still avoid 실패. Koreans use 실패 warmly in encouragement: 실패는 성공의 어머니 ('failure is the mother of success'). Pitfall: like 성공, do not use 을/를 for the domain — 사업을 실패했어요 is wrong; it's 사업에 실패했어요. And for flunking a test, prefer 떨어지다 over 실패.

mistakes: Using 을/를 for the area of failure: 사업을 실패했어요 is wrong. The particle is 에: 사업에 실패했어요.
Saying 시험에 실패했어요 for 'I failed the exam'. Far more natural is 시험에 떨어졌어요. Reserve 실패 for broader goals/projects.
Confusing 실패 (a failed outcome) with 실수 (a momentary slip). Forgetting your lines is a 실수; the whole project not working out is a 실패.

usage: 노력이 + adjective frames effort as the topic
I make an effort every day.
노력하다 = 'to make an effort/try hard'; noun + 하다
I put in a lot of effort.
노력을 하다 split out, with 많이 = 'a lot'
If you try hard, you can do well.
examples: 한국어를 배우려고 노력해요.
I'm making an effort to learn Korean.
-려고 = 'in order to'; the goal you exert effort toward
노력 없이는 성공도 없어요.
Without effort, there is no success either.
없이는 = 'without ~ (emphatic)'; a common motivational pairing
조금만 더 노력해 보자.
Let's try a little harder.
반말 자기 격려 / friends; 노력해 보다 = 'try making an effort'
nuance: 노력 (努力, 努 'to strive/exert' + 力 'power/strength') is literally 'to put forth strength' — sustained, earnest effort toward a goal, a warm and admired virtue in Korean culture where 노력하는 사람 ('a person who tries hard') is high praise. Its verb is 하다 (노력하다), and the most natural way to say 'try to do X' is verb-려고 노력하다 (배우려고 노력하다 = make an effort to learn). Contrast 노력 with 애 (애쓰다 = 'to take pains/struggle to do something'): 애쓰다 highlights the toil and is used to thank someone — 애쓰셨어요 ('you worked hard / thanks for your trouble') — while 노력 is the neutral noun for effort itself. Do not confuse 노력 with 노동 (勞動), which is physical 'labor/work' as in a job or workforce. Also distinguish 수고 (受苦), the 'trouble/hard work' you acknowledge in others: 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work'). Pitfall: 노력하다 is intransitive toward a goal — to say 'try TO do something' use the -려고 노력하다 frame, not a direct object; '한국어를 노력해요' is incomplete — say 한국어를 배우려고 노력해요 or 한국어 공부를 열심히 해요.

mistakes: Confusing 노력 (effort/striving) with 노동 (manual labor). 'Hard work pays off' is 노력은 배신하지 않아요; a labor union is 노동조합 — never swap them.
Saying 한국어를 노력해요 to mean 'I try at Korean'. 노력하다 needs a goal clause: 한국어를 배우려고 노력해요.
Using 노력하세요 to thank someone for their hard work. To acknowledge effort, say 수고하셨어요 or 애쓰셨어요; 노력하세요 means 'go try hard (a command)'.

usage: 차이가 크다 = 'the gap is large'; 차이 pairs with size adjectives
I can't really tell the difference.
차이를 모르다 with -겠- softening to 'I'm not sure'
noun + 차이: 나이 차이 = age difference/gap
examples: 한국어와 일본어는 차이가 있어요.
Korean and Japanese have differences.
A와 B는 차이가 있다 is the frame for comparing two things
가격 차이가 너무 커요.
The price difference is too big.
가격 차이 (price gap); 크다 expresses the magnitude
둘은 비슷해 보이지만 차이가 나요.
The two look similar, but they do differ.
차이가 나다 = 'a difference arises/shows'; 나다 = to occur
nuance: 차이 (差異, 差 'to differ' + 異 'different/unlike') is the noun 'difference/gap' between two or more things, and it lives with two verbs: 있다 ('there is a difference') and 나다 ('a difference arises/shows') — 차이가 있다 and 차이가 나다 are both natural, the latter stressing that a gap becomes apparent. It also pairs with size adjectives: 차이가 크다/적다 (big/small difference). The contrast to learn is the noun 차이 vs the verb 다르다 ('to be different'): 차이 names the gap as a thing ('there is a difference'), while 다르다 is how you actually say two things 'are different' — '한국어는 일본어와 달라요' (Korean is different from Japanese). English speakers often try to turn 차이 into the predicate ('they are difference'), but you need either 차이가 있다 (noun) or 다르다 (adjective-verb). Also distinguish 차이 (the gap itself) from 차이점 (the specific point/respect in which they differ): 두 제품의 차이점을 알려 주세요 = tell me the specific differences. Pitfall: do not say 차이해요 — 차이 has no verb form; use 차이가 나다/있다 or switch to 다르다.
